questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] GraphQL API generated from workspace metadata (mastertwenty, twenty/fabledocs3/adr-006-generated-graphql-single-pipeline.md). Scenario: a CRM hosts 10,000 workspaces, and each one defines its own custom objects and fields; across the fleet about 1,200 self-serve schema changes land every day, and an admin expects a new field to be usable within seconds; the clients are the typed web app, SDKs regenerated from introspection, Zapier-style integrations and REST callers, and they send arbitrary nested queries; the target is p95 under 500 ms; one integration asks for a page of 200 companies together with each company's people and opportunities. Write your design before you look: how a workspace's types and operations come into existence without hand-written resolvers, how one execution path serves every object and every facade, how a nested read avoids a query per row, what is cached per workspace and what makes that cache move on when a field is added, which limits stop a careless or hostile query, how domain errors reach clients, and where record permissions are enforced. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Derive the operations, never write them: for every object in the workspace's metadata the server registers one resolver name per generic query and mutation method, and that name map sends each top-level field to its object and method. A custom object is servable as soon as its metadata exists, with no resolver code per object.

[w3] Run every operation through one shared pipeline: the common query runner throttles, validates the arguments, parses the selection against the metadata, applies pre-query hooks, checks complexity, runs inside the caller's workspace context before enriching the results. At this pin the runner lives under api/common rather than inside the GraphQL module, so a fix there covers every caller.

[w3] Answer N+1 with batch loading per level: for each selected relation the runner collects the parent ids and issues one IN (...) query over all of them, with a single row cap for that batch. A page of 200 companies with people and opportunities is a handful of queries, not one query per company.

[w3] Key the generated schema text by version instead of deleting it: the printed SDL and its scalar list are stored under workspace id plus metadata version (plus application), and on a miss they are regenerated from the flat metadata and written back. A schema change moves the version, so the next request simply misses and rebuilds.

[w3] Put the query guards in the shared runner, where every facade passes: it refuses a one-to-many relation nested inside another one-to-many, and it rejects a selection whose relation-based complexity exceeds a configured ceiling. A nested read can widen but cannot multiply level after level.

[w2] Translate errors at one boundary: domain code throws typed exceptions, and the API catch passes each one through a single switch that maps it by class (permission, ORM, throttling, query runner, auth and so on) to a GraphQL error with a stable code. Anything the switch does not know is rethrown untouched.

[w2] Keep authorization below the API: before running, the runner resolves the caller's role permission config and asks the data source for a repository bound to it, so object and field restrictions are applied by the data layer for GraphQL, REST and MCP alike instead of being repeated in each resolver.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same CRM six months later: two admins in one workspace add fields within the same second, and an integration that regenerates its typed client from introspection starts writing records with the new fields; a reporting job pages contacts with a very large `first` and selects each contact's notes; an old code path throws a plain Error underneath a record query; and compliance attaches a new check to the company updateOne hook just before a bulk-edit feature ships. What breaks, how would you notice, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The record path and the schema text drift apart: a record query is answered from the workspace cache's resolver map and flat object and field maps, and the printed SDL plays no part in executing it. A write with a new field can succeed while the regenerated client still lacks it, or the other way round; monitor the two for disagreement instead of assuming one cache.

[w3] Two simultaneous schema changes can lose a version bump: the increment reads the workspace row's version and then writes that value plus one in a separate update, with no lock, so both changes may write the same number. An SDL generated between them is then cached under the final version without the second field. Make the bump a single atomic increment, or bump once after the last change commits.

[w3] GraphQL find-many uses `first` itself as the page size and only falls back to the default when it is omitted, then fetches one extra row to detect a next page. A client asking for 50,000 contacts gets a 50,001-row query, so the page ceiling has to be enforced in the runner.

[w2] Nested lists scale with the parent page: the batch for a relation is capped at a per-parent allowance times the number of parents, in one shared query. A huge parent page makes a huge notes query, and because the cap is shared, a few parents with thousands of notes can crowd their siblings out of the batch. Window per parent and price complexity by expected rows, not relation count.

[w2] The REST facade clamps its limit to the shared maximum while the GraphQL path does not, so two facades over one runner promise different ceilings. A limit enforced in only one facade is exactly the kind of drift the single pipeline was meant to prevent.

[w2] The record path builds its own error responses: when the class switch rethrows an exception it does not recognize, the formatter returns that error's own message with a generic internal code. A plain Error or an untranslated driver failure can therefore show internal text to the client. Replace unknown messages with a standard one and report the original.

[w2] Hooks are found by object and method, and the only wildcard is 'any object, this method', so a check attached to company updateOne never runs for updateMany, mergeMany or a restore. A bulk edit built on updateMany skips it silently. Register the check on every write method of the object, and test each generated mutation against the hook registry.

[w1] On the record path, only the number of root fields and duplicate roots are checked again before execution; the field-count ceiling configured for the parse phase is not part of this path. Do not count on that plugin for record queries, and keep the real budget in the runner.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your API design against the alternatives: one static records endpoint that takes an object name and a JSON filter, hand-written resolvers backed by dataloaders, generating each tenant's schema at deploy time, a REST implementation with its own data path, GraphQL versus REST as the product's main surface, and one global schema that stores custom fields in a JSON column. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A single static records endpoint needs no generation machinery, but every custom object becomes untyped JSON to its clients: nothing to introspect, nothing to generate types from, and no server-side checking of filters. Generation costs real infrastructure and buys first-class typed objects.
keyPoints.quote: no introspection of custom objects, no codegen'd frontend types

keyPoints.text: [w3] Hand-written resolvers with dataloaders cannot exist for objects that are defined at runtime. The generic path instead checks each method's arguments with its own assertion and builds the resolver from the workspace context, then the runner plans the whole read. The cost is that you re-implement part of GraphQL execution yourself (argument checks, shaping the selected fields).
[w2] Deploy-time generation per tenant would make the schema a build artifact, which breaks the promise that an admin's change is usable at once; that requirement is what forces runtime generation.
keyPoints.quote: edits must be live in seconds (ADR-002's product promise)

keyPoints.text: [w2] What runtime generation costs: every active workspace has its own schema to build and hold, and staleness in that cache stops being a performance question and becomes wrong answers. Price it with version keys, drift monitoring and a bounded build cost per workspace.
keyPoints.quote: the API's shape is effectively a cache entry

keyPoints.text: [w2] A REST stack with its own data path doubles every permission and soft-delete rule and guarantees drift. Translating REST onto the shared runner costs REST some idiom (status codes, limits), and policy still has to live in the runner, or the facades drift anyway.
keyPoints.quote: two data paths means permissions and soft-delete implemented twice

keyPoints.text: [w2] GraphQL fits a product whose shape differs per customer: clients introspect their own workspace and fetch a nested read in one request. Integrations still want plain URLs and docs, so REST and OpenAPI stay as facades rather than as a second API.
keyPoints.quote: needs REST for integration ergonomics and OpenAPI docs

keyPoints.text: [w1] A global schema with a JSON custom-fields column avoids per-workspace types and DDL, but custom fields then lose typed columns, real foreign keys and cheap per-field indexes, so they filter and aggregate worse than built-in ones. The per-workspace schema is the supporting decision that makes generated, typed APIs possible.
